title: Second and third normal forms
description: A practical guide to separating partial and transitive dependencies in a hypothetical retail order dataset without losing the meaning of order headers, line items, products, and customers.
lead: Second and third normal forms solve different problems that often appear together in order data. Second normal form asks whether a non-key fact depends on only part of a composite key. Third normal form asks whether a non-key fact depends on another non-key fact instead of depending directly on the key. This article uses a small hypothetical retail order fixture to separate those two cases and show where each attribute belongs.

sections.heading: Start with the key, not with the table name
paragraphs: Assume a hypothetical retail dataset arrives as one wide relation named order_line_extract. Each row represents one purchased SKU on one order. The natural row identifier is the pair order_id and sku, because one order can contain several SKUs and one SKU can appear on many orders. For this example, assume a given SKU appears at most once per order. If the source permits duplicate lines for the same SKU on the same order, line_number or another line identifier would need to be part of the key instead.

The important candidate key for this example is therefore order_id, sku. Every non-key attribute should be checked against that whole key before deciding whether the table is in second or third normal form.

Here is the hypothetical starting relation: order_line_extract(order_id, sku, order_date, customer_id, customer_email, customer_tier, product_name, category_id, category_name, quantity, unit_price_at_order).

The relation is already shaped as rows, not repeating columns, so this guide does not cover first normal form. The problem here is dependency placement. Some facts describe the order, some describe the product, some describe the customer, some describe the category, and some describe the order line itself.
bullets: Candidate key for the starting relation: order_id, sku.
Line-level facts: quantity and unit_price_at_order depend on the order and the SKU together.
Order-level facts: order_date and customer_id depend on order_id alone.
Product-level facts: product_name and category_id depend on sku alone.
Customer and category descriptors introduce third-normal-form questions after second normal form has been addressed.

sections.heading: Second normal form: remove partial dependencies
paragraphs: Second normal form is about full dependence on a composite key. If a table has a single-column key, partial dependency is not the issue. If the key is composite, each non-key attribute must depend on the whole key, not on just one component of it.

In the hypothetical order_line_extract relation, order_date depends on order_id, not on the pair order_id, sku. Repeating order_date on every line of an order creates an update anomaly: correcting the date for order 1001 requires changing every line for that order. The same is true for customer_id. The value is chosen by the order header, not by each product line.

Product facts have the symmetric problem. product_name depends on sku alone. category_id also depends on sku alone in this example. Repeating product_name on every order line creates the possibility that SKU MUG-RED is called “Red mug” on one historical line and “Red ceramic mug” on another. That inconsistency is not an order-line fact; it is a misplaced product fact.

A second-normal-form decomposition separates the facts whose determinants are order_id and sku from the facts whose determinant is the whole composite key. At this stage, the tables can be orders_2nf(order_id, order_date, customer_id, customer_email, customer_tier), products_2nf(sku, product_name, category_id, category_name), and order_lines_2nf(order_id, sku, quantity, unit_price_at_order).

Notice one deliberate choice: unit_price_at_order stays on order_lines_2nf. A common mistake is to move price to products because price sounds product-related. But in an order dataset, the price charged for a SKU can vary by order because of promotions, contracts, markdowns, taxes, or historical price changes. In this example, unit_price_at_order is determined by the pair order_id, sku, not by sku alone. Moving it to products would replace a historical line fact with a current product attribute.
bullets: Partial dependency: order_id determines order_date and customer_id even though the table key is order_id, sku.
Partial dependency: sku determines product_name and category_id even though the table key is order_id, sku.
Not a partial dependency in this example: order_id, sku determines quantity and unit_price_at_order.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL-style SQL based on the hypothetical example.
-- It expresses the 2NF split; it is not evidence of execution.

CREATE TABLE orders_2nf (
  order_id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  order_date date NOT NULL,
  customer_id integer NOT NULL,
  customer_email text NOT NULL,
  customer_tier text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE products_2nf (
  sku text PRIMARY KEY,
  product_name text NOT NULL,
  category_id integer NOT NULL,
  category_name text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE order_lines_2nf (
  order_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES orders_2nf(order_id),
  sku text NOT NULL REFERENCES products_2nf(sku),
  quantity integer NOT NULL,
  unit_price_at_order numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, sku)
);

sections.heading: Third normal form: remove transitive dependencies
paragraphs: After the second-normal-form split, two tables still carry a different kind of problem. The orders_2nf table has customer_email and customer_tier. Those attributes are not partial dependencies because orders_2nf has a single-column key, order_id. But they are still not facts about the order if customer_id determines them.

The dependency chain is order_id determines customer_id, and customer_id determines customer_email and customer_tier. That means order_id determines customer_email and customer_tier through another non-key attribute. This is a transitive dependency.

The products_2nf table has the same pattern if category_id determines category_name. The chain is sku determines category_id, and category_id determines category_name. category_name is therefore transitively dependent on sku through category_id.

Third normal form removes those transitive dependencies by creating referenced tables for the intermediate determinants. The revised design is orders(order_id, order_date, customer_id), customers(customer_id, customer_email, customer_tier), products(sku, product_name, category_id), categories(category_id, category_name), and order_lines(order_id, sku, quantity, unit_price_at_order).

This does not mean every descriptive text value must be split into its own table. The split is justified by a dependency claim. If customer_tier is assigned per customer, then customer_tier belongs with customers. If a tier is recalculated per order at purchase time and intentionally frozen, then it may belong with orders under a different name, such as customer_tier_at_order. Normalization follows the business meaning of the fact, not the English noun in the column name.
bullets: Transitive dependency in orders_2nf: order_id determines customer_id, and customer_id determines customer_email and customer_tier.
Transitive dependency in products_2nf: sku determines category_id, and category_id determines category_name.
In this order-data example, third normal form keeps descriptive non-key attributes dependent on keys rather than on other non-key attributes.

sections.heading: Counterexamples that separate the two normal forms
paragraphs: The distinction becomes clearer when the same attribute is tested in two different places.

Counterexample 1: customer_email in the original order_line_extract table violates more than one idea, but the first thing to notice is the partial dependency through order_id. Because order_id determines customer_id for the whole order, and the customer values repeat on every line, the wide table is not in second normal form. After customer information is moved out of order_lines and order headers, the remaining question is third normal form: does customer_id determine customer_email? If yes, customer_email belongs in customers.

Counterexample 2: category_name in the original table may look like a product detail, but the determinant matters. If sku determines category_id and category_id determines category_name, then category_name is not directly a SKU fact. In a 2NF-only design, products_2nf still repeats category_name for every product in the same category. Renaming “Drinkware” to “Kitchen drinkware” would require updating many product rows. Third normal form puts the name in categories.

Counterexample 3: unit_price_at_order should not be normalized away merely because a product table exists. Suppose order 1001 sold SKU MUG-RED for 12.00 and order 1002 sold the same SKU for 10.00 during a promotion. Those two rows do not contradict the dependency order_id, sku determines unit_price_at_order. They contradict the incorrect dependency sku determines unit_price_at_order. The correct design keeps the charged price on the line item.

Counterexample 4: product_name may be a product fact in this simplified model, but some retail systems store product_name_at_order to preserve the label shown to the customer at checkout. That would be a different attribute with different semantics. product_name belongs to products only if the model intends the current product name. product_name_at_order belongs to order_lines or another order snapshot structure if the model intends historical display text.

sections.heading: A diagnostic for proposed dependencies
paragraphs: A dataset cannot prove a functional dependency for all future data, but it can disprove one with a counterexample. The following illustrative query uses a small hypothetical fixture and looks for determinants that map to more than one dependent value.

The expected result for the first diagnostic is no rows for order_id determining order_date and customer_id in the sample. That supports, but does not prove, the modeling assumption that those are order-header facts. The expected result for the unit_price_at_order diagnostic is SKU MUG-RED, because the same SKU appears with two prices. That is useful evidence against placing unit_price_at_order in products.

Use this diagnostic as a modeling aid, not as a substitute for business rules. If the data contains bad historical records, a query may show violations of a rule that is still intended to be true. If the sample is too small, a query may miss violations that appear later. The durable decision comes from both observed data and the declared meaning of the attributes.
bullets: Ask: what is the determinant?
Check whether the determinant is the whole key, part of the key, or another non-key attribute.
Treat query results as counterexample search, not mathematical proof.
Name historical snapshot attributes explicitly when they differ from current master data attributes.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative dependency diagnostic using a hypothetical retail fixture.
-- These queries show the reasoning pattern; they are not evidence of execution.

WITH order_line_extract(order_id, sku, order_date, customer_id, customer_email,
                        customer_tier, product_name, category_id, category_name,
                        quantity, unit_price_at_order) AS (
  VALUES
    (1001, 'MUG-RED',  DATE '2026-01-05', 501, 'ana@example.test', 'gold',   'Red mug',   20, 'Drinkware', 2, 12.00),
    (1001, 'TEA-BLK',  DATE '2026-01-05', 501, 'ana@example.test', 'gold',   'Black tea', 30, 'Tea',       1,  8.50),
    (1002, 'MUG-RED',  DATE '2026-01-06', 502, 'bo@example.test',  'silver', 'Red mug',   20, 'Drinkware', 1, 10.00),
    (1003, 'KETTLE-1', DATE '2026-01-07', 501, 'ana@example.test', 'gold',   'Kettle',    20, 'Drinkware', 1, 35.00)
)
SELECT order_id
FROM order_line_extract
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT order_date) > 1
    OR COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) > 1;

WITH order_line_extract(order_id, sku, order_date, customer_id, customer_email,
                        customer_tier, product_name, category_id, category_name,
                        quantity, unit_price_at_order) AS (
  VALUES
    (1001, 'MUG-RED',  DATE '2026-01-05', 501, 'ana@example.test', 'gold',   'Red mug',   20, 'Drinkware', 2, 12.00),
    (1001, 'TEA-BLK',  DATE '2026-01-05', 501, 'ana@example.test', 'gold',   'Black tea', 30, 'Tea',       1,  8.50),
    (1002, 'MUG-RED',  DATE '2026-01-06', 502, 'bo@example.test',  'silver', 'Red mug',   20, 'Drinkware', 1, 10.00),
    (1003, 'KETTLE-1', DATE '2026-01-07', 501, 'ana@example.test', 'gold',   'Kettle',    20, 'Drinkware', 1, 35.00)
)
SELECT sku, COUNT(DISTINCT unit_price_at_order) AS observed_price_count
FROM order_line_extract
GROUP BY sku
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT unit_price_at_order) > 1;

sections.heading: A compact decision rule
paragraphs: For a composite-key order-line table, second normal form is the first pass: remove attributes that depend only on order_id or only on sku. This creates order headers, product references, and true line facts. Third normal form is the second pass: within each resulting table, remove attributes that depend on a non-key attribute rather than directly on the table key.

A useful phrasing is: 2NF asks whether the fact needs all of the key; 3NF asks whether the fact is being reached through another fact. In the example, order_date does not need all of order_id, sku, so it fails 2NF in the original table. customer_email is reached through customer_id after the order table exists, so it fails 3NF there. unit_price_at_order needs the order and the SKU together, so it remains a line fact.

The goal is not to maximize the number of tables. The goal is to make each stored fact live at the grain where it is true. Once the grain is explicit, constraints and joins can express the relationships: order lines reference orders and products, orders reference customers, and products reference categories. That model makes anomalies easier to spot because a change to a customer, product, or category has one natural place to occur.

takeaways: Second normal form removes non-key attributes that depend on only part of a composite key, such as order_date depending on order_id inside an order_id, sku table.
Third normal form removes non-key attributes that depend on another non-key attribute, such as customer_email depending on customer_id inside an orders table.
Do not move historical line facts, such as unit_price_at_order, into a product table unless the business rule really says SKU alone determines the value.
Dependency diagnostics can find counterexamples in sample data, but the final model still depends on declared business meaning.

title: Rounding residuals in proportional allocations
description: A practical rule for allocating integer units proportionally without losing or creating units through rounding.
lead: Proportional allocation becomes risky when the output must be stored in indivisible units: cents, impressions, seats, points, whole items, or integer basis points. If each row is rounded independently, the rows may not add back to the original total. The fix is to calculate the residual explicitly and distribute the remaining units by a deterministic rule.

sections.heading: Why independent rounding breaks totals
paragraphs: A proportional allocation starts with a total amount and a set of weights. For example, an order-level discount may be allocated to order lines by each line’s share of pre-discount merchandise value. A shared operating cost may be allocated across stores by sales. A usage credit may be allocated across customers by events. In dimensional models, allocated facts are a normal pattern; the Kimball Group describes allocation as a way to place higher-grain values at a lower fact-table grain for analysis. The modeling idea is separate from the arithmetic problem: once the target unit is indivisible, proportional shares usually contain fractions.

The failure mode is simple. Suppose a hypothetical retail order has a 100 cent promotion discount and three equal-weight lines. The exact proportional shares are 33.333..., 33.333..., and 33.333... cents. If each row is rounded down or rounded to the nearest cent under ordinary half-up expectations, the stored values are 33, 33, and 33. The detail rows now add to 99 cents, even though the header discount is 100 cents. If each exact share is rounded up, the rows become 34, 34, and 34, adding to 102 cents. Neither answer is acceptable if downstream reconciliation expects the line-level allocation to preserve the header total.

The same issue appears when allocating counts rather than money. If 10 seats are distributed by fractional usage shares, the system cannot assign 3.4 seats to one row and 6.6 to another. It must assign whole units. Any method that rounds each row independently can create or destroy units because it ignores the aggregate constraint.
bullets: Input total: the integer number of units that must be preserved, such as 100 cents.
Weights: nonnegative quantities used to determine proportional shares.
Exact quota: target total multiplied by a row’s weight share, before whole-unit allocation.
Base allocation: the rounded-down whole-unit part of the exact quota.
Residual: the remaining units after summing base allocations.

sections.heading: Use a largest-remainder rule
paragraphs: A reliable allocation rule is to round every exact quota down first, then distribute the leftover units to the rows with the largest fractional remainders. This is the same basic idea used by largest-remainder apportionment methods: assign lower quotas first, then give the remaining indivisible units to the largest fractional parts until the total is exhausted.

For a positive target total, the rule is: compute each row’s exact quota; assign the floor of that quota; compute the residual as target minus the sum of floors; sort rows by fractional remainder descending; add one unit to the first residual rows. If the target total is negative, allocate the absolute value using the same rule, then reapply the sign. This avoids confusing behavior around floor, truncation, and remainder operations on negative numbers.

This rule gives a useful counterexample to a tempting shortcut: putting the entire residual on the first row. Suppose the target is 10 units and the weights are 49, 49, and 2. The exact quotas are 4.9, 4.9, and 0.2. The floor allocations are 4, 4, and 0, leaving a residual of 2. If the residual is dumped onto the first row, the result is 6, 4, 0. The total is preserved, but the first row is 1.1 units above its exact quota while the second row has the same fractional claim to an extra unit. The largest-remainder result is 5, 5, 0, which is reconciled and keeps each row at either the floor or ceiling of its exact quota.

Ties are not a nuisance detail. In real pipelines, ties happen frequently because weights are repeated, rounded upstream, or stored in common units such as cents. The allocation must define a stable tie-breaker, such as line sequence, source-system row id, or a published business priority. Without that tie-breaker, two runs over the same data can preserve the same total while assigning the residual to different rows.
bullets: Do not round each row independently and then hope the detail sum matches the header.
Do not hide the residual in an arbitrary row unless the business rule explicitly says to do that.
Do compare fractional remainders and use a deterministic tie-breaker.
Do store or be able to reproduce the allocation rule used for a published fact table.

sections.heading: Worked hypothetical retail example
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail order with a 100 cent order-level discount. The business rule is to allocate the discount to lines in proportion to each line’s pre-discount extended price, measured in cents. The order has four lines: A has weight 999, B has weight 499, C has weight 299, and D has weight 203. The total weight is 2,000 cents.

The exact quotas are calculated as target times line weight divided by total weight. Line A receives 100 × 999 ÷ 2,000 = 49.95 cents. Line B receives 100 × 499 ÷ 2,000 = 24.95 cents. Line C receives 100 × 299 ÷ 2,000 = 14.95 cents. Line D receives 100 × 203 ÷ 2,000 = 10.15 cents. These exact quotas add to 100 cents, but none of the first three can be stored exactly as whole cents.

Round down first. The base allocations are 49, 24, 14, and 10 cents. The base sum is 97 cents, so the residual is 3 cents. The fractional remainders are 0.95, 0.95, 0.95, and 0.15. Lines A, B, and C have the largest remainders. Because A, B, and C are tied, the rule uses line sequence as the tie-breaker. The final allocated discount cents are A = 50, B = 25, C = 15, and D = 10. The detail sum is 100 cents, exactly matching the original order discount.

This example also shows why the rule should be stated in units, not display formatting. The unit being preserved is the cent, not the printed dollar amount. If the warehouse stores dollars as decimal values with two fractional digits, the same allocation still needs to be performed in cent-level units or an exact decimal representation. Binary floating-point arithmetic is a poor fit for this kind of reconciliation because decimal fractions may be stored as approximations. Exact numeric or integer minor-unit representations are easier to reason about for allocation totals.
bullets: Target discount: 100 cents.
Weights: 999, 499, 299, and 203 cents.
Exact quotas: 49.95, 24.95, 14.95, and 10.15 cents.
Base allocations: 49, 24, 14, and 10 cents.
Residual: 3 cents.
Final allocations using line sequence as tie-breaker: 50, 25, 15, and 10 cents.

sections.heading: Implementation pattern with integer arithmetic
paragraphs: The cleanest implementation is often to avoid fractional comparison entirely. For each row, calculate numerator = absolute_target_units × weight_units. The base allocation is the integer quotient of numerator divided by total_weight_units. The remainder numerator is numerator modulo total_weight_units. Rows with larger remainder numerators have larger fractional remainders because they all share the same denominator.

The following PostgreSQL-style SQL is illustrative; it has not been executed here. It assumes a single allocation group, a target measured in integer units, nonnegative weights, and a nonzero total weight. It uses a stable line sequence as the tie-breaker. In production-style models, the same pattern is normally partitioned by allocation group, such as order_id, invoice_id, accounting_period, or customer_event_batch_id. Use integer or numeric types wide enough for the intermediate product of target units and weight units.

PostgreSQL 18 documents numeric as an exact numeric type of selectable precision and describes real and double precision as inexact floating-point types. PostgreSQL 18 also documents integer division and modulo behavior for mathematical operators. The example below casts the product to numeric before quotient and remainder calculations so the intended arithmetic is explicit and less dependent on narrow integer ranges.

codeExamples.code:
WITH line_items(line_seq, sku, weight_units) AS (
    VALUES
        (1, 'A', 999),
        (2, 'B', 499),
        (3, 'C', 299),
        (4, 'D', 203)
),
header AS (
    SELECT 100 AS target_units
),
prepared AS (
    SELECT
        li.line_seq,
        li.sku,
        li.weight_units,
        h.target_units,
        CASE WHEN h.target_units < 0 THEN -1 ELSE 1 END AS target_sign,
        ABS(h.target_units) AS abs_target_units,
        SUM(li.weight_units) OVER () AS total_weight_units
    FROM line_items li
    CROSS JOIN header h
),
parts AS (
    SELECT
        line_seq,
        sku,
        weight_units,
        target_units,
        target_sign,
        abs_target_units,
        total_weight_units,
        FLOOR(
            (abs_target_units::numeric * weight_units::numeric)
            / total_weight_units::numeric
        ) AS base_abs_units,
        MOD(
            (abs_target_units::numeric * weight_units::numeric),
            total_weight_units::numeric
        ) AS remainder_num
    FROM prepared
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT
        *,
        abs_target_units - SUM(base_abs_units) OVER () AS residual_units,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            ORDER BY remainder_num DESC, line_seq ASC
        ) AS remainder_rank
    FROM parts
)
SELECT
    line_seq,
    sku,
    target_sign * (
        base_abs_units + CASE WHEN remainder_rank <= residual_units THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
    ) AS allocated_units
FROM ranked
ORDER BY line_seq;

sections.heading: Diagnostics and edge cases
paragraphs: A proportional allocation should be tested at the allocation-group grain, not just across a whole table. If discounts are allocated by order, then every order’s allocated line sum must match its order-level discount. A table-wide sum can pass while individual orders are wrong in opposite directions. The reconciliation query should group by the same key used to define the target total.

The first diagnostic is conservation: sum allocated units equals target units for every group. The second diagnostic is quota distance: after sign normalization, each row should receive either the floor or the ceiling of its exact absolute quota. The third diagnostic is deterministic ordering: if two rows have the same remainder, the allocation should still be reproducible from stored columns. These checks catch accidental changes, such as replacing integer division with nearest rounding or omitting the tie-breaker from a window function.

Zero weights need an explicit policy. If all weights are zero and the target is also zero, every row can receive zero. If all weights are zero and the target is nonzero, there is no proportional answer because no row has a positive claim on the total. The pipeline should reject the group, route it to an exception table, or use a different business rule such as equal allocation. Do not silently divide by zero or assign the amount to the first row without labeling that as a non-proportional fallback.

Negative targets should be normalized before allocation. For example, if returns are stored as negative cents, allocate the absolute number of cents, then multiply the final allocations by negative one. This keeps the residual distribution rule identical for charges, credits, discounts, and reversals.

Finally, keep allocation policy separate from tax, revenue recognition, or accounting advice. This article covers numeric representation and aggregation behavior: preserving a total while distributing indivisible units. Whether a particular allocated fact is legally, financially, or operationally appropriate depends on the domain policy that chose the target, weights, and grain.
bullets: Reconcile at the same grain as the allocation target.
Use exact integer or decimal arithmetic for target units and weights.
Reject or explicitly handle groups with nonzero targets and zero total weight.
Define a deterministic tie-breaker and treat it as part of the business rule.
For negative totals, allocate the absolute value and then restore the sign.

codeExamples.code:
SELECT
    allocation_group_id,
    MAX(target_units) AS target_units,
    SUM(allocated_units) AS allocated_units,
    MAX(target_units) - SUM(allocated_units) AS difference_units
FROM allocated_detail
GROUP BY allocation_group_id
HAVING MAX(target_units) <> SUM(allocated_units);

sections.heading: Where this fits in a data model
paragraphs: The allocation rule should live next to the fact definition, not as an undocumented report calculation. If a line-level fact table contains allocated discount cents, allocated freight cents, or allocated usage units, the model should identify the original target grain, the allocation weights, the preserved unit, and the deterministic tie-breaker. That documentation is part of the business rule, not an implementation footnote.

This is especially important when facts are exposed in multiple units of measure. A model may store a standard unit and derive alternate views through conversion factors, but the preserved total still needs a declared unit for reconciliation. If cents are the preserved unit, reconcile cents. If whole scan units are preserved, reconcile scan units. Do not rely on formatted display values to prove that the stored fact is balanced.

takeaways: Rounding each proportional row independently can lose or create units, even when every row appears locally reasonable.
Round down first, compute the residual, and give the remaining units to the largest fractional remainders with a deterministic tie-breaker.
Integer quotient and modulo arithmetic provide a practical implementation pattern for largest-remainder allocation.
Validate allocations at the target grain, and make zero-weight and negative-target behavior explicit.
Document the preserved unit, allocation weights, and tie-breaker as part of the fact-table business rule.

title: Division by zero in business ratios
description: A practical guide to modeling business ratios so undefined results are not confused with true zero performance.
primaryKeyword: Division by zero in business ratios
relatedKeywords: Division by zero in business ratios
lead: A business ratio can be zero, nonzero, undefined, or invalid. Treating all four cases as one numeric value creates misleading dashboards: a channel with no traffic can look like it performed at 0%, and a data defect can be hidden inside a total. The fix is to model the numerator, denominator, computed value, and calculation status separately.

sections.heading: The problem with zero denominators
paragraphs: Business ratios compress two measurements into one value. Conversion rate divides orders by sessions. Average order value divides revenue by orders. Refund rate divides refunds by purchases. The ratio is useful only when the denominator represents a real opportunity set. If the opportunity set is empty, the ratio is not zero; it is undefined.

That distinction matters because zero performance and no opportunity imply different actions. If an email campaign had 100 sessions and 0 orders, its conversion rate is exactly 0%. Someone may need to inspect the offer, landing page, or audience. If a partner channel had 0 sessions and 0 orders, the conversion rate is not 0%; there was no denominator to evaluate. Calling both rows 0% says the same operational event happened when it did not.

A third case is worse: a zero denominator with a nonzero numerator. If a row shows 0 sessions and 4 orders for a session-based conversion rate, the ratio is undefined and the inputs are inconsistent for that metric definition. That could be caused by late-arriving session data, a join-grain problem, a bot filter difference, or an order attribution rule that does not match the session population. The correct output is not 0%, and it is not infinity. It is an invalid or unresolved calculation state.

The modeling rule is simple: do not ask a single numeric column to carry both the value and the reason the value may not exist. Store the inputs, compute the ratio only when defined, and expose a status that distinguishes true zero performance from undefined or invalid cases.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail counterexample
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail dashboard that reports daily conversion rate by acquisition channel. The metric definition is orders divided by sessions at the channel-day grain. Four rows are enough to show the common failure modes.

The email row has 100 sessions and 0 orders. Its conversion rate is 0 divided by 100, or 0.0000. That is a defined zero. The search row has 200 sessions and 20 orders, so its conversion rate is 20 divided by 200, or 0.1000. The partner row has 0 sessions and 0 orders. Its conversion rate is not 0.0000; it is undefined because no sessions occurred. The affiliate row has 0 sessions and 4 orders. Under this metric definition, that is an invalid input combination because orders are being counted where there is no denominator population.

Now compare three ways to produce the daily total. The valid ratio-of-sums calculation includes rows with a positive denominator and divides total valid orders by total valid sessions: 20 divided by 300, which equals 0.0666667, or about 6.67%. It also reports one undefined row and one invalid row beside the value. That tells the reader both the metric value and the completeness of the population behind it.

A naive total can hide the invalid row by summing all numerators and all denominators: 24 divided by 300 equals 0.0800, or 8.00%. That looks precise, but it silently counted affiliate orders without affiliate sessions. Another naive approach sets undefined and invalid row-level rates to zero and averages row rates: email 0.0000, search 0.1000, partner 0.0000, affiliate 0.0000, average 0.0250. That 2.50% number is not the channel-day conversion rate; it is an average of mixed calculation states.

The counterexample demonstrates two rules. First, do not coerce undefined ratios to zero. Second, aggregate the numerator and denominator at the reporting grain, then divide, rather than averaging precomputed row-level ratios unless the business definition explicitly calls for an unweighted average.
bullets: Defined zero: denominator is positive and numerator is zero.
Defined nonzero: denominator is positive and numerator is positive.
Undefined: denominator is zero and numerator is zero, so there was no population to evaluate.
Invalid or unresolved: denominator is zero and numerator is nonzero, so the inputs do not satisfy the metric definition.

sections.heading: Use a calculation contract, not just a formula
paragraphs: A robust ratio needs a small contract that can be implemented in SQL, a semantic layer, or a metrics service. The contract should state the numerator, denominator, valid grain, allowed signs, aggregation rule, and output statuses. For this article, negative denominators and corrections are outside the scope; the examples assume nonnegative counts for sessions and orders.

The contract for the hypothetical retail conversion rate can be written as follows. The numerator is orders. The denominator is sessions. The valid calculation grain is any grain where both inputs have been aggregated to the same population. The rate is orders divided by sessions only when sessions is greater than zero. If sessions is greater than zero and orders is zero, the rate is a real numeric zero. If sessions and orders are both zero, the rate value is null and the status is undefined_no_denominator. If sessions is zero and orders is nonzero, the rate value is null and the status is invalid_zero_denominator_nonzero_numerator.

This separates the human-readable status from the numeric value. A null rate is not automatically bad; it can mean the ratio is mathematically undefined for a legitimate reason. A zero rate is not automatically missing; it can be a real business result. The status tells downstream consumers which interpretation is correct.

It is also useful to store or publish diagnostic counts next to the metric. A dashboard tile that says conversion rate is 6.67% with one invalid segment is more honest than a tile that says 8.00% after silently mixing incompatible rows. The invalid count does not have to block every report, but it should be visible enough to prevent false confidence.

If many ratios share statuses, model those statuses consistently. A small calculation-status dimension or enumerated field can keep terms such as defined_zero, defined_nonzero, undefined_no_denominator, and invalid_input consistent across metrics. Keep the field specific to calculation status rather than creating a broad catch-all dimension. Kimball Group guidance warns against abstract generic dimensions in dimensional models because unlike concepts often have different attributes and generic abstraction can reduce legibility.

sections.heading: Illustrative PostgreSQL pattern
paragraphs: The following SQL is an illustrative PostgreSQL 18 style example, not a claim of execution. It uses numeric inputs so the division result can preserve decimal precision appropriate for reporting. PostgreSQL documents numeric and decimal as exact numeric types of selectable precision, while real and double precision are inexact floating-point types. PostgreSQL also documents that aggregate functions such as sum return null when no rows are selected, except for count. That behavior is relevant when filtered aggregates have no contributing rows.

The example keeps the raw numerator and denominator, classifies each row, and then computes a daily valid conversion rate from rows with a positive denominator. It also counts undefined and invalid rows so the total cannot hide them.

codeExamples.code:
with channel_day as (
    select *
    from (values
        (date '2026-10-01', 'email',     100::numeric,  0::numeric),
        (date '2026-10-01', 'search',    200::numeric, 20::numeric),
        (date '2026-10-01', 'partner',     0::numeric,  0::numeric),
        (date '2026-10-01', 'affiliate',   0::numeric,  4::numeric)
    ) as v(metric_date, channel, sessions, orders)
), classified as (
    select
        metric_date,
        channel,
        sessions,
        orders,
        case
            when sessions is null or orders is null then 'missing_input'
            when sessions < 0 or orders < 0 then 'invalid_negative_input'
            when sessions = 0 and orders = 0 then 'undefined_no_denominator'
            when sessions = 0 and orders <> 0 then 'invalid_zero_denominator_nonzero_numerator'
            when sessions > 0 and orders = 0 then 'defined_zero'
            when sessions > 0 and orders <> 0 then 'defined_nonzero'
        end as rate_status,
        case
            when sessions > 0 then orders / sessions
            else null
        end as conversion_rate
    from channel_day
), daily_total as (
    select
        metric_date,
        sum(orders) filter (where sessions > 0) as valid_orders,
        sum(sessions) filter (where sessions > 0) as valid_sessions,
        sum(orders) filter (where sessions > 0)
            / nullif(sum(sessions) filter (where sessions > 0), 0) as valid_conversion_rate,
        count(*) filter (where rate_status = 'defined_zero') as defined_zero_rows,
        count(*) filter (where rate_status = 'undefined_no_denominator') as undefined_rows,
        count(*) filter (where rate_status = 'invalid_zero_denominator_nonzero_numerator') as invalid_rows
    from classified
    group by metric_date
)
select *
from daily_total;

sections.heading: Expected result and diagnostics
paragraphs: For the hypothetical fixture, the positive-denominator rows are email and search. Their valid orders are 0 plus 20, which equals 20. Their valid sessions are 100 plus 200, which equals 300. The valid daily conversion rate is therefore 20 divided by 300, or 0.0666667. There is one defined-zero row, one undefined row, and one invalid row.

Those diagnostics are not decorative. They answer different operational questions. The defined-zero count tells you how many populations had measurable opportunity but no outcome. The undefined count tells you how many populations had no denominator and should not be interpreted as failures. The invalid count tells you where the metric inputs conflict with the definition and may need upstream investigation.

A common display mistake is to replace every null conversion rate with 0.00% because a charting tool handles zero more conveniently than null. That is acceptable only if the label still preserves the distinction, for example by displaying not applicable for undefined rows and data issue for invalid rows. If the visual layer cannot preserve the distinction, the data model should provide separate fields such as conversion_rate_value and conversion_rate_status rather than a single formatted string.

Another mistake is to materialize only the row-level ratio and discard numerator and denominator. Once the inputs are gone, higher-level aggregation becomes ambiguous. A regional conversion rate cannot be safely computed by averaging store-level rates unless the intended metric is explicitly an unweighted average of stores. For ordinary business conversion, the safer model keeps additive inputs available and performs division after aggregation.

The same pattern applies beyond conversion rate. Revenue divided by customers is undefined when customers equal zero. Cost per acquisition is undefined when acquisitions equal zero. Defect rate is a true zero when inspected units are positive and defects are zero; it is undefined when inspected units are zero. Each metric needs its own numerator and denominator definitions, but the calculation states are reusable.

sections.heading: Implementation checklist
paragraphs: Before publishing a business ratio, ask whether a consumer can tell the difference between zero performance and no denominator. If not, the model is incomplete. The remedy usually does not require a large framework. It requires preserving additive inputs, using null for undefined numeric values, and carrying a status that explains why the value is null or zero.

For batch models, classify rows at the lowest grain where the numerator and denominator are both meaningful. For reporting models, aggregate additive inputs to the requested grain and divide once. For semantic layers, make the ratio expression use null-safe division and expose invalid or undefined counts as companion measures. For exports, avoid sending only a formatted percentage; include numerator, denominator, value, and status whenever the data will be reused.

The most important tradeoff is strictness. A strict metric may exclude invalid zero-denominator rows from the published rate and surface an invalid count. A permissive metric may include all numerators and denominators and rely on separate data quality processes. For ratios used in operational decisions, strictness is usually easier to explain because the published number only reflects rows that satisfy the metric definition. If invalid rows are material, the report should say so rather than absorbing them into the rate.

Do not turn this into a general data quality checklist. The specific modeling problem is narrower: division produces a valid business ratio only when the denominator represents a nonempty population for that metric. Once that is explicit, undefined results and actual zero performance stop competing for the same numeric value.
bullets: Keep numerator and denominator as first-class fields.
Use null for undefined or invalid ratio values, not zero.
Add a calculation status that distinguishes defined_zero, defined_nonzero, undefined_no_denominator, and invalid_input.
Aggregate additive inputs first; divide at the reporting grain.
Publish diagnostic counts so invalid rows cannot be hidden inside a total.

takeaways: Zero performance requires a positive denominator and a zero numerator; a zero denominator is not zero performance.
A ratio model should expose numerator, denominator, value, and calculation status instead of relying on one numeric field.
For ordinary weighted business ratios, aggregate the numerator and denominator first, then divide once at the reporting grain.
Rows with zero denominator and nonzero numerator should be treated as invalid or unresolved for that metric definition, not coerced to zero.
Null ratio values are useful when paired with a status that explains whether the result is undefined, invalid, or missing.
